questions.explanation: Values within one column often repeat and share a type, which makes them highly compressible. Bitmap encoding is especially useful for low-cardinality warehouse columns: one bitmap per distinct value turns filters into fast bitwise operations while reducing bytes read.

questions.question: Define bitmap encoding precisely, and explain what is done when the bitmaps are sparse.

options.text: One bitmap per distinct value, one bit per row; sparse ones are run-length encoded
One bitmap per row with one bit per distinct value; sparse bitmaps are discarded
A hash of each value per row; sparse values fall back to plain strings
A sorted list of the distinct values; sparse columns are left unencoded

questions.explanation: The bit is 1 if the row has that value. This works because distinct values are often few compared to rows. For a product_sk column over a billion rows with 100,000 products, raw bitmaps would be 10 to the 14th bits — about 12.5 TB — hence run-length encoding. A country column may have about 200 distinct values and needs one bit per row.

questions.question: A query filters product_sk to one of three values; another filters product_sk = 31 AND store_sk = 3. What bitwise operations do these become?

options.text: A bitwise OR of three bitmaps, then a bitwise AND of two; valid because column files share row order
An AND of three bitmaps then an OR of two; validity comes from each column being sorted
Both become XOR operations over the bitmaps; validity comes from the stored checksums
Bitmap columns cannot be combined at all, so each predicate is evaluated as a separate scan

questions.explanation: The OR can be done very efficiently. The kth bit in one column's bitmap corresponds to the same row as the kth bit in another's. Bitmap indexes are very well suited to the kinds of queries common in a data warehouse.

questions.question: Cassandra and HBase are often called column-oriented. Why is that misleading?

options.text: Calling Bigtable-style column families columnar; a row's columns sit together
Calling them row-oriented, when internally they are in fact a true columnar layout
Calling them key-value stores, when their data model is really a relational one
Calling them LSM-based engines, when they actually store their data in B-trees

questions.explanation: Cassandra and HBase organize data into column families, but within a family they store a row key together with that row's columns. They therefore remain mostly row-oriented and do not use the per-column compression and scan layout associated with analytical column stores.

questions.question: Disk-to-memory bandwidth is a big bottleneck but not the only one. Which others do developers of analytical databases worry about? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Using the bandwidth from main memory into the CPU cache efficiently
Avoiding branch mispredictions and bubbles in the CPU pipeline
Making use of single-instruction-multi-data instructions in modern CPUs
Reducing the number of network round-trips to the storage layer

questions.explanation: Once disk reads are reduced, CPU efficiency matters: engines try to move data through memory caches efficiently, avoid unpredictable branches that stall pipelines, and process many values per instruction with SIMD. Vectorized execution targets all three.

optionExplanations.a: After disk I/O falls, moving column batches efficiently from main memory into CPU caches becomes a bottleneck. Cache-friendly contiguous processing reduces wasted memory bandwidth.
optionExplanations.b: Unpredictable branches can flush or stall CPU pipelines, creating bubbles even when data is already in memory. Vectorized operators reduce branch-heavy per-row control flow.
optionExplanations.c: SIMD instructions apply one operation to several values at once, increasing arithmetic throughput for scans and aggregates. Columnar batches place same-type values in a suitable layout.
optionExplanations.d: Network round trips can matter in a distributed warehouse, but they are not one of the CPU-side bottlenecks enumerated in this question. The listed concerns explain vectorized execution within a processing node.

questions.question: Define vectorized processing and explain how columnar layout helps the CPU.

options.text: Loop over an L1-resident chunk, operating on the compressed form directly
Use GPUs rather than CPUs for the aggregation work, since GPUs have wider registers
Decompress each column block first, then process the resulting rows one at a time
Spread every query across many machines so each handles a slice of the columns

questions.explanation: No function calls per record, unlike code needing calls and conditions for each. Column compression lets more rows fit in the same L1 cache. The key point: operators such as the bitwise AND and OR work on the compressed representation without decompressing first.

questions.question: What order is easiest in a column store, and what does imposing an order buy you?

options.text: Insertion order, since inserting just appends; an imposed order indexes it
Sorted order is easiest; imposing insertion order is what enables compression
Random order is easiest; imposing an order is what enables replication
Reverse insertion order is easiest; imposing an order enables deletion

questions.explanation: It doesn't necessarily matter in which order rows are stored. The alternative is to impose an order, as with SSTables, and use it as an indexing mechanism — sortedness is optional here, and when chosen it doubles as an index.

questions.question: Why can't each column be sorted independently?

options.text: Row reconstruction needs the kth item of each column to be the same row
Because sorting each column separately is computationally too expensive
Because compression algorithms require one global ordering
Because the query optimizer assumes insertion order throughout

questions.explanation: So the data needs to be sorted an entire row at a time, even though it is stored by column. Positional correspondence is the invariant that independent sorting would destroy.

questions.question: Who normally chooses a column store's physical sort order?

options.text: An administrator, based on common query patterns
The optimizer permanently rewrites physical order for every query
The engine chooses only from column cardinality
Each application query supplies a different physical sort order

questions.explanation: Physical row order is chosen ahead of time from expected workload. A leading `date_key` lets range queries skip old data; a second `product_sk` groups rows for the same product within each date, improving filters and aggregations that use both.

questions.question: Why does sorting help compression, and how does the effect decay across sort keys?

options.text: Few distinct values give long runs; later sort keys are jumbled
Sorting helps every column equally, since each column file is compressed independently
Sorting actively hurts compression, which is why insertion order is usually preferred
Sorting only improves the compression of numeric columns, not string-valued ones

questions.explanation: A simple run-length encoding could compress the first sort column to a few kilobytes even with billions of rows; columns further down the priority appear in essentially random order. Run-length encoding could compress that column to a few kilobytes even with billions of rows. Columns further down the sorting priority appear in essentially random order. But having the first few columns sorted is still a win overall.

questions.question: Whose idea was storing several different sort orders, and what makes it almost free?

options.text: C-Store, adopted by Vertica; replication already duplicates the data
Bigtable, adopted by HBase; compression makes the extra copies cheap
Dremel, adopted by Parquet; the columnar layout makes copies free
Hive; it is free simply because storage has become inexpensive

questions.explanation: Different queries benefit from different sort orders, and data needs replicating anyway so you don't lose it when a machine fails — so store that redundant data sorted differently and use whichever version fits the query. The redundancy you already pay for is repurposed for performance.

questions.question: Multiple sort orders in a column store are 'a bit similar' to what, and where does the analogy break?

options.text: Multiple secondary indexes; but column stores have no pointers, so each sort order is a full copy
Materialized views; but a view is virtual rather than an actual copy stored on disk
Table partitioning; but partitions are disjoint rather than overlapping copies
Replication; but replicas are byte-identical to one another rather than reordered

questions.explanation: A row-oriented store keeps every row in one place — the heap file or clustered index — and secondary indexes hold only pointers to matching rows. No pointers means each sort order is a complete copy, not a lightweight index.

questions.question: Why do the columnar optimizations make writes difficult? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Update-in-place, as B-trees do, is not possible with compressed columns
Inserting mid-table would mean rewriting every column file consistently
Column files cannot be appended to under any circumstances
Each write requires a distributed transaction across the column files

questions.explanation: Rows are identified by their position within a column, so an insertion has to update all columns consistently. The workload assumption that justifies all of it: most of the load is large read-only queries run by analysts.

optionExplanations.a: Compressed column files encode many values together, so overwriting one field in place can invalidate compression and positional structure. The engine instead creates new batches and merges them later.
optionExplanations.b: A row's position must correspond across every column; inserting into the middle of one file shifts that alignment. Preserving it would require coordinated rewrites of all affected column files.
optionExplanations.c: Column stores can append new batches or immutable files and later merge them, as Vertica does with an in-memory write area. The restriction is on arbitrary in-place insertion, not all appends.
optionExplanations.d: A write path may coordinate several columns, but it does not inherently require a distributed transaction for each row. Buffering and bulk merging solve the layout problem without that universal requirement.

questions.question: How can a column store avoid expensive row-by-row updates to compressed files?

options.text: Buffer writes in memory and merge them into column files later
Parquet updates column files in place with a B-tree
Hive refreshes every materialized view synchronously per row
C-Store solves writes by discarding cold columns

questions.explanation: Updating compressed column files row by row is expensive. Vertica accumulates writes in an in-memory store and periodically merges batches into new column files, applying the same buffered-write principle as an LSM-tree.

questions.question: With an in-memory write store, what must queries do, and what does the analyst perceive?

options.text: Examine disk columns and memory writes together, hidden by the optimizer
Read only the on-disk columns, leaving recent writes invisible until the next merge
Be re-run by hand once each background merge into the column files has completed
Read the in-memory store for new data only when given an explicit query flag

questions.explanation: Read-your-writes is preserved despite the two-tier storage: inserts, updates and deletes are immediately reflected in subsequent queries.

questions.question: How universal is column-oriented storage among data warehouses, and what speed advantage does it offer?

options.text: Not every warehouse is columnar, but columnar can be much faster ad hoc
That columnar storage is consistently slower for ad hoc analytic queries than rows
That every data warehouse in production use today is built as a column store
That row-oriented data warehouses are now entirely obsolete and should be migrated

questions.explanation: Column orientation is common but not universal among warehouses. For ad hoc analytics it can be much faster because a query reads only the referenced columns, those columns compress well, and vectorized execution processes them efficiently; row-oriented warehouses remain viable for other workloads.

questions.question: Which SQL aggregates are worth caching, and why?

options.text: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX; rescanning raw rows for shared aggregates is wasteful
GROUP BY and HAVING; their results are never worth caching for reuse
RANK and DENSE_RANK; caching applies only to window functions over partitions
DISTINCT and UNION; caching their results mainly saves network bandwidth

questions.explanation: Repetition across queries is what makes precomputation pay.

questions.question: Define materialized view versus virtual view, and describe what the SQL engine does when you read from each.

options.text: Virtual views expand on the fly; materialized views are a copy on disk
Materialized views are a shortcut for writing queries; virtual views are copies on disk
Both are copies written to disk, differing only in how often each is refreshed
Both are expanded on the fly at query time, differing only in whether results get cached

questions.explanation: A view is a table-like object whose contents are the results of some query. Copy on disk versus expansion at query time is the whole difference: a virtual view is just a shortcut for writing queries.

questions.question: Why must materialized views be maintained, and where do they belong?

options.text: They are denormalized copies, so writes cost more — rarely worth it in OLTP
They need no maintenance at all, since they are recomputed from scratch on every read
They belong in OLTP databases, where writes are cheap and reads are latency-critical
They must be refreshed by hand by whichever analyst originally created the view

questions.explanation: The database can update them automatically. Note the closing hedge — whether they actually improve read performance depends on the individual case.

questions.question: Give both names for the special case of a materialized view, and describe what aggregating along an axis yields.

options.text: Data cube or OLAP cube; aggregating along an axis gives one fewer dimension
Star cube or fact cube; aggregating along an axis adds a further dimension
Snowflake cube or dimension cube; aggregating along an axis returns the raw facts
Hypercube or pivot cube; aggregating along an axis yields a single scalar

questions.explanation: A data cube, also called an OLAP cube, precomputes aggregates for combinations of dimensions. Aggregating along one axis removes that dimension from the grouping—for example, summing across dates yields sales by product regardless of date.

questions.question: What is the main flexibility cost of a precomputed data cube?

options.text: It cannot filter on attributes that were not selected as dimensions
Cubes save space but slow queries, so they replace raw facts
Cubes answer arbitrary questions and require no maintenance
Cubes make detailed source data unnecessary

questions.explanation: A cube trades flexibility for lookup speed by fixing dimensions and aggregates in advance. It can answer total sales per store quickly, but not an unplanned predicate such as items priced above $100 if price was not a cube dimension. Keeping raw facts preserves the ability to ask new questions.

questions.question: Storage engines split in two by workload. Which bottleneck belongs to which?

options.text: OLTP: small key lookups bound by seek time. Analytics: scans bound by bandwidth
OLTP is bound by disk bandwidth, whereas analytics is bound by disk seek time
Both OLTP and analytics turn out to be bound by disk seek time on modern hardware
Both OLTP and analytics are bound by available CPU rather than by the disk at all

questions.explanation: OLTP is user-facing with a huge volume of requests each touching few records by key via an index. Analytics serves business analysts at much lower query volume, but each query scans many millions of records — and column-oriented storage is an increasingly popular solution.

questions.question: What is the defining difference between log-structured and update-in-place storage?

options.text: One appends immutable files; the other overwrites fixed-size pages
The schools are row and column stores, corresponding exactly to OLTP and OLAP
The schools are in-memory and on-disk
The schools are hash and sorted indexes only

questions.explanation: The deep distinction is immutability versus overwriting. Log-structured engines append and later replace whole immutable files through compaction; B-tree engines modify fixed-size pages in place, supported by write-ahead logging and concurrency control.

questions.question: What single idea do log-structured engines contribute, and why does it matter for hardware?

options.text: Turning random-access writes into sequential writes, raising throughput on both hard drives and SSDs
Eliminating secondary indexes altogether, which greatly reduces memory pressure
Compressing all stored data, which reduces the disk capacity a dataset requires
Avoiding the write-ahead log entirely, which halves the engine's write amplification

questions.explanation: Log-structured engines buffer and batch random logical updates into sequential file writes. Sequential access raises throughput on hard drives and remains useful on SSDs by reducing write amplification and improving I/O locality, even though SSD controllers already remap physical writes.

questions.question: Why are row-lookup indexes often less central—not irrelevant—for large analytical scans?

options.text: Large scans benefit more from reading fewer compressed bytes
Analytical queries almost always look up one primary key
Indexes cannot be built on fact tables
Materialized views eliminate every use for indexes

questions.explanation: Indexes still help selective analytical predicates, but many warehouse queries touch a large fraction of a table. In that case the dominant goal shifts from finding individual rows to scanning fewer columns and fewer compressed bytes efficiently.

questions.question: A developer who understands storage engine internals but has never built one can do what, and not what?

options.text: Choose an engine and reason about its tuning knobs, but not tune one expertly
Implement a production-grade storage engine, with no remaining gaps in skill
Tune any engine to expert level, though OLAP internals stay out of reach
Predict exact query latency from first principles, without any benchmarking

questions.explanation: You can imagine what effect a higher or lower value may have, and it has hopefully given you enough vocabulary and ideas to make sense of the documentation for the database of your choice — matching the promise made at the start: a rough idea of what the engine is doing under the hood.
